newsitem.title: USA: NYS voters approve of Pataki, but not for taxes.
newsitem.headline: NYS voters approve of Pataki, but not for taxes.

text.p: New York Gov George Pataki got high marks from voters, with his latest ranking matching levels seen in November, even though they do not like how he has handled education and taxes, a new poll said Tuesday.

"The governor wins solid approval in every area except education--a constant concern--and taxes, an even more constant concern. And low approval on the tax issue should be of some concern to Pataki," said Maurice Carroll, director of the Quinnipiac College Polling Institute.

The Republican governor has trumpeted his Administration's efforts to reduce taxes, most recently with an ambitious, $3.5 billion plan to help reduce school property taxes over five years. Another program he proposed would reduce estate and gift taxes.

However, Pataki has said it would be difficult to begin phasing out this year the state's tax on clothing that costs more than $500. A one-week moratorium on the state's 4.0 percent levy, which was matched by most localities, including New York City, in January proved popular. The plan was pushed by the Democrat-led Assembly.

The poll highlighted a few other of Pataki's vulnerabilities, as in New York City, which has nearly half the state's population, the same percentage of voters approved of the governor as disapproved of him, splitting 44 to 44 percent. The biggest concentration of Pataki supporters was found in the suburbs, followed by upstate.

Pataki got his highest ratings from voters for his policies on crime, welfare and the environment. But the 1,071 New Yorkers who were surveyed from February 24 to March 2 were much more evenly divided over Pataki's performance when it comes to the budget, as only 45 to 42 percent approved.
The Pataki Administration last year set a national record for late budgets, failing to reach a pact with lawmakers until 104 days past the April 1 deadline.
With taxes, the governor's approval margin slips to 45 to 44 percent, and a slim majority of voters disapproved of Pataki's education policies, by 45 to 43 percent.

Another soft spot was seen in how the governor was perceived, as only 38 to 53 percent said Pataki was sympathetic to the problems of the poor. Still, by a big margin of 71 to 24 percent, the New Yorkers polled said Pataki "can get things done," and 62 to 28 percent found him likeable.
